title: Week 3 · Lesson 8: Respiratory Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 3 — Lesson 8: Respiratory Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal: Determine whether dyspnea reflects an oxygenation, ventilation, perfusion, hemoglobin, or cardiac-output problem—and recognize when outpatient assessment is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate ventilation, oxygenation, oxygen content, and tissue oxygen delivery.
  • Apply alveolar ventilation and V/Q concepts to common disease.
  • Distinguish hypoxemia from tissue hypoxia.
  • Build a mechanism-based acute dyspnea differential.
  • Recognize respiratory-failure red flags requiring emergency escalation.

Part 1 — Five Questions for Dyspnea

Ask: Is air reaching alveoli? Is blood reaching alveoli? Is diffusion impaired? Is hemoglobin sufficient? Is cardiac output adequate?

Ventilation moves air. Oxygenation transfers oxygen into arterial blood. Oxygen delivery depends on oxygen content and cardiac output. A normal SpO₂ does not prove adequate hemoglobin or perfusion.

Part 2 — Alveolar Ventilation and CO₂

Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate. Rapid shallow breathing can produce poor effective ventilation. Alveolar hypoventilation causes CO₂ retention and can produce respiratory acidosis.

Think hypoventilation with opioid/sedative effect, CNS disease, neuromuscular weakness, severe fatigue, obesity-related hypoventilation, or severe airflow limitation.

Part 3 — V/Q and Shunt

Effective exchange needs both Ventilation and pulmonary Q perfusion.

High V/Q/dead-space physiology: ventilation with too little perfusion, classically PE.

Low V/Q: perfusion exceeds ventilation, common in airway obstruction and many parenchymal diseases.

Shunt-like physiology: blood passes nonventilated/collapsed or fluid-filled alveoli, such as pneumonia, atelectasis, or pulmonary edema.

Part 4 — Hypoxemia vs Hypoxia

Hypoxemia is low arterial oxygen. Hypoxia is inadequate tissue oxygen availability/utilization. Severe anemia or shock can cause tissue hypoxia despite a reassuring pulse-oximeter saturation.

Major hypoxemia mechanisms: V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion limitation, hypoventilation, and low inspired oxygen.

Part 5 — Clinical Patterns

Asthma/COPD: airflow obstruction, mucus, and bronchoconstriction create low-V/Q regions; rising fatigue, altered mental status, or worsening CO₂ retention are dangerous.

Pneumonia: alveolar exudate reduces ventilation to perfused regions; fever and focal symptoms may help but do not establish severity.

PE: perfusion falls to ventilated alveoli; sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, syncope, tachycardia, hypoxemia, and VTE risk raise concern.

Pulmonary edema/HF: increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure moves fluid toward alveoli, increasing diffusion distance and work of breathing.

Pneumothorax: loss of lung expansion; sudden pain/dyspnea and instability require urgent consideration.

Part 6 — FNP Assessment and Disposition

Assess onset, triggers, fever/cough, pleuritic or ischemic chest symptoms, VTE risk, orthopnea/edema, medications/sedatives, exposures, prior lung/heart disease, vital signs, work of breathing, mental status, ability to speak, oxygenation, and focused cardiopulmonary exam.

Testing should answer a question: ECG, chest imaging, infection testing, blood count, blood gas in appropriate acute-care settings, and VTE/heart-failure pathways may be relevant.

Emergency: severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, altered mental status, exhaustion, hypotension, syncope, rapidly worsening hypoxemia, suspected PE/ACS/pneumothorax, or signs of severe asthma/COPD/HF/infection.

Part 7 — Board-Style Cases

A patient with Hb 6.5 g/dL and SpO₂ 98% can still have low oxygen content and tissue hypoxia: saturation is not hemoglobin concentration.

A postoperative patient with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia needs emergency evaluation for possible PE—not reassurance from an apparently clear lung examination.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Ventilation removes CO₂. Alveoli exchange gases. V/Q mismatch is common; PE is high V/Q, pneumonia/edema are low-V/Q or shunt-like.

FNP decision: identify the dangerous mechanism and trajectory; escalate immediately for respiratory failure or time-sensitive cardiopulmonary disease.
